newsitem.title: JAPAN: No Korea breakthrough seen from release of American.
newsitem.headline: No Korea breakthrough seen from release of American.

text.p: The release of a young American in North Korea could help Pyongyang mend fences with Washington, but is unlikely to herald a major breakthrough in reducing tensions on the Korean peninsula, analysts said on Wednesday.
North Korea on Wednesday freed American Carl Hunziker who had been detained in the communist state for three months on espionage charges.
Hunziker, who his family says is a missionary, arrived in Tokyo with U.S. Congressman Bill Richardson, who negotiated his release.
Political analysts in Tokyo said although the release of Hunziker, 26, could help North Korea improve ties with the United States, it would not win Pyongyang any points with arch rival South Korea.
"The gap in strategy between the United States and South Korea could even widen after the release," said Masao Okonogi of Tokyo's Keio University.

Tense relations between the two Koreas have worsened since a North Korean submarine landed 26 agents on a South Korean beach in September. Twenty-four of them were shot dead, one was captured alive and another is still at large.
South Korea demanded an apology from Pyongyang over the submarine incursion and assurances that such an incident would not be repeated.
In a move that angered the Stalinist state, President Kim Young-sam said Seoul would never have a dialogue with the North until there was an apology over the submarine incident.

"President Kim's remarks pushed the two Koreas deeper into stalemate," Noriyuki Suzuki, analyst at the Tokyo-based Radiopress news agency, said. "It would be extremely difficult for President Kim to retract the remarks."
Pyongyang insists the submarine incident was an accident and demands the return of the bodies and the captured agent.

At a meeting of Asia-Pacific leaders in the Philippines, President Bill Clinton and President Kim on Sunday called on Pyongyang to take unspecified "acceptable steps" to end a crisis caused by the North's submarine incursion.

"My sense is that the North Korean government wants to get the submarine incident behind it and re-engage with the international community," Congressman Richardson told reporters in Tokyo after bringing back Hunziker from Pyongyang.
Keio University's Okonogi said there remained a glimmer of hope that the two Koreas could break the ice and work towards reducing tensions on the Korean Peninsula.
"The situation would quickly turn for the better if North Korea apologises and South Korea returns the bodies of North Korean soldiers," Okonogi said.
Clinton and Kim also on Sunday renewed an invitation to North Korea to join four-nation peace talks, which would also involve China.
"As long as the two Koreas remained at odds with each other, the four-nation talks would never get going," Radiopress' Suzuki said.
Okonogi said there could be a new era in relations in mid-1997 when North Korea's leader-in-waiting Kim Jong-il was expected to take formal control of the communist state.

Kim Jong-il, 54, who is supreme commander of North Korea's 1.1 million-strong military, has yet to be formally confirmed in the two key posts held by his late father Kim Il-sung -- general secretary of the ruling Workers' Party and state president.
